name: Design an API Gateway
intent: Build the front door for dozens of services: proxy every request with well under a millisecond of overhead, apply authentication, quotas and transformations in one place, and change its configuration without dropping a connection.
codeTitle: a shared rate limiter with local approximation, and a retry budget
finalIntro: One authenticated API call through the gateway, and a retry that the budget allows.
prompt: Design an API gateway like Kong, Envoy or AWS API Gateway. It sits in front of about 60 internal services and handles 20,000 requests per second at the peak. It must route by host, path and header, terminate TLS, authenticate callers, enforce a quota for every consumer, spread load over healthy instances of each service, support API versions and canary releases, and pick up configuration changes without dropping connections. It must add very little latency, and it must not be a single point of failure.
functional: Route requests to a service by host, path prefix, method and header
Terminate TLS and keep pooled connections to the upstream services
Run a chain of plugins: authentication, authorization, rate limiting, request and response transformation, caching and logging
Discover the healthy instances of each service and balance load across them
Retry failed calls safely, and stop calling a service that is failing
Route by API version, and send a small share of traffic to a canary
Enforce a request quota per consumer
Apply configuration changes while traffic is flowing
nonFunctional: Add under 1 ms at the median and under 5 ms at the 99th percentile to each request
Handle 20,000 requests per second at the peak, and scale by adding instances
Survive the loss of any single gateway instance or a whole availability zone with no outage
A configuration change reaches every instance within seconds and never drops an open connection
The gateway keeps serving with its last good configuration if the control plane is down
A quota is enforced to within a few percent across all instances
A slow or failing service must not drag the whole gateway down with it

firstAttempt.text: No gateway at all. Clients call each service directly, and every service terminates its own TLS, checks the token, applies its own rate limit and writes its own access log. Public addresses and ports are published for every service.
limits: Sixty services each implement authentication and rate limiting, in several languages, and they drift apart
Every service is exposed to the internet, so each one needs hardening and a certificate
A quota for a consumer cannot be enforced across services, because each service counts alone
Moving a path to another service, or splitting traffic for a canary, means changing every client
There is no single place to see who called what, or to switch off an abusive consumer

nodes.label: Each service does its own checks

steps.title: Put one front door in front of every service
steps.problem: Each service terminates its own TLS and repeats the same checks, and callers need to know where every service lives.
steps.fix: Run a reverse proxy, the data plane, as the only public entry. It terminates TLS once, so internal calls can use a cheaper connection. It matches each request against a route table: host first, then the longest path prefix, then method and headers, such as 'api.example.com, /orders/* goes to the orders cluster'. It keeps a pool of warm, keep-alive connections to each upstream, and with HTTP/2 many requests share one connection, so a call does not pay a new TCP and TLS handshake, which is one to three round trips. It is built on an event loop, so one instance holds tens of thousands of idle client connections.
steps.tradeoff: Callers see one address and services stay private. Every request now takes an extra hop, which costs roughly 0.1 to 0.3 ms inside a data center, and the gateway becomes something every request depends on, which the later steps must deal with.

steps.title: Run the cross-cutting checks as a plugin chain
steps.problem: Authentication, quotas, caching and logging should be written once, but they cost time on every request.
steps.fix: Requests pass through an ordered chain of plugins, also called filters: authenticate, authorize, rate limit, transform the request, look in the cache, call the upstream, transform the response, and log. Each plugin can short-circuit the chain with a response, such as 401 or 429, so rejected traffic never reaches a service. Order matters: cheap checks come first and an unauthenticated caller must not consume quota. Authentication verifies a signed JWT locally with public keys that were fetched once and cached, which takes tens of microseconds, instead of calling the identity provider for every request, which takes milliseconds and adds a dependency to every call. A cache plugin answers repeatable GET requests from memory.
steps.tradeoff: One place to enforce policy, and a cheap local check keeps the overhead small. A signed token cannot be revoked before it expires, so tokens are short-lived or a small deny list is pushed to the gateway, and every plugin that makes a remote call adds its round trip to every request.

steps.title: Discover instances, balance load, and protect against failure
steps.problem: Services come and go as they scale and deploy, and one slow instance can hold up everything that calls it.
steps.fix: The gateway learns the list of healthy instances for each service from a service registry, which can be a platform API or DNS. It picks an instance with a load-balancing rule such as 'least outstanding requests' or 'the better of two random choices', which avoids sending more work to an instance that is already slow. Active health checks probe every few seconds, and passive outlier detection ejects an instance after several consecutive errors. Every call has a timeout. A circuit breaker stops calling a service that is failing. A failed call to an idempotent endpoint is retried on a different instance, but only within a retry budget, for example no more retries than 10 percent of the requests sent in the last few seconds.
steps.tradeoff: A bad instance is routed around within seconds, and a failing service gets room to recover. Retries without a budget turn one slow service into three times the load, which makes the slowdown worse. Timeouts, ejections and budgets are numbers to tune, and wrong values cause either needless errors or no protection.

steps.title: Run many stateless instances with shared quotas
steps.problem: One gateway instance cannot carry 20,000 requests per second, and a single instance is a single point of failure, but each caller has a quota that all instances must respect together.
steps.fix: Run many identical instances in several availability zones behind a layer 4 load balancer. They keep no per-request state and read the same configuration, so any of them can serve any request, and each one is sized so the rest can absorb the loss of one zone. A quota that must hold across instances is counted in a shared store such as Redis. Calling it on every request adds a round trip of about 0.5 ms and 20,000 operations per second. Instead, each instance counts locally and synchronizes with the store every 100 ms, or takes a lease of tokens in advance. If the store is unreachable, instances fall back to local limits and keep serving.
steps.tradeoff: Capacity grows by adding instances, and the loss of one is invisible. A quota becomes approximate: with a 100 ms sync an abusive caller can exceed the limit by roughly the traffic of one sync interval, and a limit split evenly between instances wrongly rejects a caller whose traffic is uneven. The shared store must be sized and itself made highly available.

steps.title: Separate the control plane and apply changes without a restart
steps.problem: Routes, plugins, keys and quotas change many times a day, and a restart to apply a change would drop thousands of live connections.
steps.fix: Split the product in two. The control plane stores the desired configuration, validates it, and pushes versioned snapshots to the data plane over a long-lived stream, as Envoy's xDS protocol does. It also relays endpoint lists from the registry. Each gateway builds the new route table beside the old one, swaps a pointer, and lets requests in flight finish on the old table, so no connection is dropped. It acknowledges the version, or rejects a bad one and keeps running the old one. The same routes carry versioning and canaries: '/v1/' and '/v2/' paths or an 'X-API-Version' header choose a cluster, and a weighted route sends 5 percent of traffic to the canary, rolled forward or back with one change.
steps.tradeoff: Changes go live in seconds and the data plane does not depend on the control plane for serving, so an outage of the control plane freezes configuration but does not stop traffic. A bad configuration can break every route at once, so changes need validation, a staged rollout and quick rollback, and instances can briefly disagree on the version.

steps.title: Keep the overhead small and make it observable
steps.problem: The gateway sees every request, so one slow plugin or one synchronous log write slows all of them, and nobody can tell where the time goes.
steps.fix: Set a latency budget for the chain, for example 1 ms at the median, and measure each plugin against it. Keep remote calls out of the hot path: verify tokens locally, cache decisions, and send access logs and trace spans to a queue in batches from a background thread rather than writing them inside the request. Propagate a trace id to every upstream so a slow request can be followed through services. Export metrics per route, per consumer and per upstream: request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, retry counts, and circuit breaker state. Alert on the gateway's own error rate and on saturation, not on the services behind it.
steps.tradeoff: The overhead stays in the range of a fraction of a millisecond, and one dashboard shows which consumer or service is the problem. Logging asynchronously means the last few records can be lost if an instance crashes, and per-consumer metrics can grow in cardinality if they are not bounded.

failures.impact: No new routes, keys or quotas can be applied, and the registry changes can no longer be relayed.
failures.answer: The data plane never needs the control plane to serve a request. Each instance keeps running with the last accepted snapshot and its cached endpoint list. Health checks continue locally, so an instance that dies is still ejected. Instances that start while it is down take the snapshot from a local file or from a peer. Fix the control plane, and the instances reconnect and catch up to the latest version.

failures.scenario: The shared counter store is unavailable
failures.impact: Quotas cannot be checked against the global count, and a strict design would reject all traffic.
failures.answer: Decide per route whether to fail open or closed. Most APIs fail open to each instance's local limit, which is the quota divided by the number of instances, and raise an alert, so callers keep working and an abuser is still contained. Strict routes, such as paid actions, fail closed for a short time. A replica takes over, and the counters restart from zero, which briefly allows a little extra traffic.

failures.scenario: A service slows down and callers retry
failures.impact: Each timeout leads to up to three more attempts, so the slow service receives up to four times its normal load and cannot recover, even after the original cause is gone.
failures.answer: Retry only idempotent calls, with a per-try timeout, backoff with jitter, and a budget that caps retries at about 10 percent of recent traffic. A circuit breaker opens when the error rate stays high, so calls fail fast for a few seconds and the service gets quiet. Limits on concurrent requests and pending requests per upstream shed the excess early instead of queueing it.

failures.impact: A wrong route or a broken plugin setting could send all traffic to the wrong place within seconds.
failures.answer: Validate every change before it is stored, by checking the schema and loading it in a test instance. Each gateway rejects a snapshot it cannot load and keeps the old one. Roll configuration out in stages, to one instance and then one zone, while watching error rates, and keep the last several versions so a rollback is one command.

failures.scenario: The identity provider rotates its signing keys
failures.impact: Tokens signed with the new key fail verification until the gateways know the new public key.
failures.answer: Gateways fetch the published key set and cache it, refetching when they see an unknown key id, at most once a minute so a flood of bad tokens cannot overload the provider. The provider publishes the new key before it starts signing with it, and the old key stays published until its tokens expire. If the provider is down, the cached keys keep working.

alternatives.title: How the gateway is deployed

options.name: One shared edge gateway
options.pro: Simple, with one place for TLS, authentication and quotas
options.con: Every team shares its blast radius and its release schedule

options.name: A gateway per team or per domain
options.pro: Teams change their own routes, and a failure stays local
options.con: Policies drift, and there is more to operate

options.name: A sidecar proxy beside every service (service mesh)
options.pro: Also covers service-to-service calls, with mutual TLS
options.con: Many more proxies to run, and extra latency on every internal hop

alternatives.pick: A shared edge gateway for outside callers, and a mesh later if internal calls need the same policy.

alternatives.title: How tokens are checked

options.name: Verify a signed JWT locally
options.pro: Tens of microseconds and no dependency on a remote service
options.con: Cannot be revoked before expiry without a deny list

options.name: Introspect each token with the identity provider
options.con: A network call on every request, and the provider must handle the full request rate

options.name: Introspect, but cache the answer for a short time
options.pro: Much less load, and revocation lags by only the cache time
options.con: More moving parts and a stale window

alternatives.pick: Local JWT verification with short-lived tokens and a pushed deny list.

alternatives.title: How quotas are counted

options.name: Central counter on every request
options.con: A round trip and a store operation for every request, and the store is a dependency

options.name: Local counters with the limit split between instances
options.con: Wrongly rejects callers whose traffic is uneven, and allows too little

options.name: Local counters synchronized every 100 ms or token leases
options.pro: Close to exact with a fraction of the store traffic
options.con: Can exceed the limit by about one sync interval of traffic

alternatives.pick: Local counters with a short sync, and strict central counting only for paid or billing quotas.

alternatives.title: How configuration reaches the data plane

options.name: Edit a file and reload the process
options.con: Reloads are slow to coordinate across many instances, and mistakes spread by hand

options.name: Poll a database for changes
options.pro: Easy to build, since instances are independent
options.con: Changes arrive after the polling interval and the database is loaded by every instance

options.name: Push versioned snapshots over a stream (xDS)
options.pro: Seconds to apply, acknowledged per instance, and no restart
options.con: Needs a control plane that is itself reliable

alternatives.pick: A pushed stream with acknowledgements, and a file on disk as the fallback.

roles.label: Gateway
roles.description: The data plane: routing, TLS and the plugin chain.

roles.label: Control plane and logs
roles.description: Configuration pushes and the log queue.

roles.label: Services and identity
roles.description: Upstream services, the canary and the identity provider.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Service registry, shared counters, cache and the config store.

quiz.question: At 20,000 requests per second the gateway calls the identity provider to introspect every bearer token. This adds about 3 ms to each request and the provider is overloaded. Which change keeps the overhead small and still handles revocation?
options: Cache each introspection answer for an hour, so the identity provider sees only a small share of the calls
Scale the identity provider ten times, so that introspection stays fast even at the full request rate
Verify signed JWTs locally, use short-lived tokens, and push a small deny list for revoked ones
Remove the check at the gateway and let each of the 60 services validate its own tokens when it needs to
quiz.explanation: Local signature checks take tens of microseconds and need no remote call, and a short lifetime plus a deny list bounds the revocation delay. An hour of caching would keep revoked tokens valid for up to an hour. More provider capacity still leaves a network call in every request.

quiz.question: Each consumer has a quota of 6,000 requests per minute across all gateway instances. The latency budget is 1 ms at the median, and a Redis call costs about 0.5 ms. Which design meets the quota within a few percent at this budget?
options: Count locally on each instance and sync with the shared store about every 100 ms, accepting a small overshoot
Call the central counter on every request, so that the count is always exact and the answer is final
Give each of 10 instances an equal local share of 600 per minute and use no shared store at all
Sync with the shared store every 10 seconds, which cuts the load on the store by a factor of 100
quiz.explanation: A 100 ms sync is under 0.2 percent of the minute, so the overshoot is tiny and the store is off the hot path. A call per request spends half the latency budget and makes the store a hard dependency. Equal shares wrongly reject callers with uneven traffic, and a 10 second sync can overshoot by far more than a few percent.

quiz.question: An upstream service slows down and starts timing out. The gateway retries each timed-out call up to 3 times, so the service gets up to 4 times its normal load and keeps failing even after the original cause is gone. Which change fixes this?
options: Raise the per-try timeout to 30 seconds, so fewer calls time out and need a retry in the first place
Scale the slow service to four times its capacity ahead of time, so that it can absorb all the retries
Retry every method, including POST, but spread the attempts with random delays so they do not align
Cap retries to idempotent calls at about 10 percent of traffic, and add a circuit breaker
quiz.explanation: A retry budget caps the extra load, and the breaker lets the service rest while callers fail fast. A 30 second timeout holds connections open and queues work behind them. Scaling out is slow and costly, and retrying non-idempotent calls can repeat side effects like double charges.
